That's basically the approach that a certain Canadian leader took in 2015, and it worked out very well for him (his party went from 35 seats to 185 seats, and won a majority government).

It was one of his early announcements (grassroots party members indicated their support for legalization in 2012, and then the leader announced it as official party policy in 2014), so everyone heard about it.  But when the actual 2015 election campaign started, but it wasn't emphasized that much in the actual campaign messaging, and instead they highlighted other issues.

For example, his campaign's TV ads and flyers would focus on getting the economy back on track, cutting taxes for middle class and raising taxes on the rich, investing more in transportation infrastructure, and so on.  From what I saw, they rarely focused on marijuana.

And IMO that was smart, because with a hot-button issue like that, you want to motivate those who support it, without firing up those who oppose it.

By simply having it in their platform, those who strongly *support* legalization would hear about it one way or another, even those who don't follow politics very closely (through word-of-mouth, through the internet, etc.), and could vote with that in mind.  For example, at a major city's annual pot rally in 2015 (which attracts thousands of pot-smokers every year), there was a giant banner with the leader's face, encouraging people to vote for him to get legalization.

Meanwhile, those who were opposed would probably be aware of it but they weren't being constantly reminded about it, so they might still decide to vote Liberal based on other issues.

I presume they also didn't want to make it seem like it was their #1 priority, and that the leader was out of touch with the issues that the public cared most about (economy, infrastructure, etc).

When asked about it in debates or interviews, the leader would say that prohibition has failed the country because our children have nearly the highest rates of marijuana usage in the world, and that it should be legalized and regulated, to "keep pot out of the hands of children, and keep profits out of the hands of criminals".

That was the basic messaging he used, and he never went far beyond that; he never tried to downplay its harms or say it's not as dangerous as people think, he just said that prohibition failed and legalization would work better.

Plus, simply having the issue on the table caused the opposing party to make some unforced errors.  For example, the incumbent prime minister said in an interview that "marijuana is infinitely worse than tobacco", and it made him sound really ignorant and out of touch.  And for their part, the opposing party actually didn't talk that much about marijuana during the campaign, because they seemed to realize that it was a tricky one that could divide their support base.  Instead, they focused on targeting anti-marijuana ads to specific communities they believed were against it.

So anyway, long story short, the ruling party's 2015 campaign is one that the US Democrats should look to for some lessons, if they try to run an election in 2018 or 2020 with marijuana legalization in their platform.

And since it'll be legalized in Canada in summer 2018, I wonder if that'll change the political dynamics in the US at all.  I'm interested to see.

I think you misunderstand what a national statistical agency means by those terms (which is probably a common mistake).

* Employment Rate = % of the adult population that is employed.  The "adult population" considered here includes people in the Labour Force (workers and those looking for work) as well as those outside the Labour Force (retirees, students, stay at home parents, or anyone else).

* Unemployment Rate = % of the *Labour Force* that is unemployed.  The work force consists only of people who have a job, or people who are looking for a job.  It does not include retirees, stay at home parents, or other people who don't want to work right now.

That's why those two numbers don't add up to 100% (if that was your concern), it's because they're measuring different things.  Unemployment rate only includes people who want to work, whereas employment rate (in this context) includes everybody, including people who retired 20 years ago.

I can understand why that would be confusing though, especially since those terms aren't defined anywhere on that webpage.

The employment rate is generally somewhere in the 60-65% range, and the unemployment rate is generally somewhere in the 5-10% range.

For December, the numbers are:

* Adult Population - 30,058,900

* Employment - 18,647,500

18,647,500/30,058,900 = 0.62, so we get an employment rate of 62.0%

* Labour Force - 19,777,900

* Unemployment - 1,130,400

1,130,400/19,777,900 = 0.057, so we get an unemployment rate of 5.7%
A government statistical agency didn't make an error, the original poster just misunderstood how the categories are calculated. See my other post in response to theirs, explaining how it works.

Well the economic impact of raising minimum wages is mixed, with some positives and some negatives.  Higher wages are a challenge for businesses, but they also increase people's incentive to work, lead to healthier and happier employees, and increase consumer spending, which is good economically.  In economics there's no clear evidence on whether or not minimum wage increases hurt overall job growth and economic growth, as some studies have found that they do, and some found that they don't.  

With corporate tax increases, it's inherently lowering the companies' profits and return-on-investment, so you could argue that a large tax hike would make a North American country a less desirable place to invest and locate businesses, especially for industries that compete globally.  That's a negative for the economy.

Now the positive side of corporate taxes is that they generate revenue, which can be used in useful ways.  In this case they would fund a generous minimum income, which would be helpful for the recipients but actually reduces their incentives to work (and thus likely reduce a North American country's labour force), which would have some negative impacts on the economy overall.

TL;DR: lower wages, and higher benefits to those not working, would discourage labour force participation to some extent, which is negative for the economy.  

From the business side, they benefit from the lower wages, but would be hurt by having higher taxes and less workers available.

I think that number is too low. I did some searching, and a large commercial airliner (as an example) can have fuel capacity of around 200,000 L ([source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_747-400)).

Jet fuel weighs 0.8 kg/L, and 1 tonne is 1000 kg, so a large commercial airliner can carry **160 tonnes of jet fuel**.

A flight from a major city in Canada to a major city in Germany is about 10.5 hours ([source](https://www.travelmath.com/flying-time/from/Vancouver,+Canada/to/Frankfurt,+Germany)), and the large commercial airliner apparently burns about 10-11 tonnes of fuel per hour ([source](https://www.flightdeckfriend.com/ask-a-captain/how-much-fuel-does-a-jumbo-jet-burn/)), so we would expect it to burn **at least 105 tonnes of jet fuel**.

For our calculations, let's suppose it was fully fueled and they dumped all extra fuel before landing, meaning the full **160 tonnes** was used. 

Apparently a large commercial airliner can have a max passenger capacity of 416 or 524 (depending on layout) so let's assume **400 passengers.**

That would mean **0.4 tonnes of jet fuel per passenger**.

The **ratio of CO2 emissions to jet fuel is 3.0** (ie. 1 kg of jet fuel burned, reacting with the oxygen in the air, produces 3 kg of CO2 emissions) ([source](https://www.engineeringtoolbox.com/co2-emission-fuels-d_1085.html)).  Therefore, we get **1.2 tonnes of CO2 emissions per passenger.**

So based on that, the estimate of 1.3 tonnes of CO2 emissions per passenger seems to be in the right ballpark, even if it might be high (depending on our assumptions, type of plane, etc.)
